title: PCOS Renamed PMOS in Global Shift That Could Transform Diagnosis for Millions
excerpt: A 14-year international effort has officially rechristened polycystic ovary syndrome as polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, acknowledging the condition's far-reaching metabolic and hormonal effects beyond the ovaries.
body:
• Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) has been renamed polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS) to better reflect the condition's complexities.
  • The name change follows a 14-year effort involving over 56 organizations and extensive input from patients and healthcare professionals worldwide.
  • The previous name misrepresented the condition, as many diagnosed patients do not have pathological ovarian cysts but rather excess antral follicles.
  • An estimated 70% of women with PMOS remain undiagnosed, highlighting the need for improved awareness and diagnosis.

The most common endocrine disorder in women no longer carries the name it has had for decades. On May 12, a global consortium of researchers, clinicians, and patient organisations announced that polycystic ovary syndrome — PCOS — will be replaced by polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS, according to a landmark policy paper published in The Lancet.

The decision, unveiled at the European Congress of Endocrinology in Prague, caps a 14-year effort involving 56 academic, clinical, and patient organisations, more than 14,000 survey responses from patients and healthcare professionals across every world region, and input gathered through modified Delphi methods, workshops, and marketing analyses.

Why the Name Had to Go

The central problem with "polycystic ovary syndrome" was that it told the wrong story. The word "cystic" implied pathological ovarian cysts, but many diagnosed patients never have them. What appear on ultrasounds are actually excess antral follicles — small, fluid-filled sacs containing immature eggs — not abnormal cysts.

"Renaming this condition is more than semantics; it's about finally recognizing the full reality of what patients experience."

— Dr Melanie Cree, pediatric endocrinologist, University of Colorado Anschutz

The old name funnelled the condition into a narrow gynaecological box. In practice, PMOS is a multisystem disorder: insulin resistance, obesity, cardiovascular risk, depression, anxiety, eating disorders, acne, and excess hair growth all feature prominently. There is currently no U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved treatment specifically for the condition, and an estimated 70% of affected women worldwide remain undiagnosed, according to the WHO.

"What we now know is that there is actually no increase in abnormal cysts on the ovary, and the diverse features of the condition were often unappreciated," Professor Helena Teede, director of the Monash Centre for Health Research and Implementation in Australia and a lead author of the Lancet paper, said in a statement.

What Changes — and What Doesn't

The condition itself, its diagnostic criteria, and existing treatments remain the same. What shifts is the framing. By foregrounding "polyendocrine" and "metabolic," the new name directs attention to the hormonal and metabolic dysfunction that drives much of the morbidity — including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, fatty liver disease, and endometrial cancer.

A study published this month in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology & Women's Health, analysing U.S. health insurance data for over 413,000 women with PMOS, found that patients faced a four-fold higher risk of cardiovascular disease compared with matched controls — a finding researchers say underscores why the metabolic framing matters.

Plans to transition to PMOS over the next three years are already underway. The WHO and the International Classification of Diseases are expected to formally adopt the terminology by 2028. Clinical guidelines, medical education curricula, and diagnostic codes will be updated in parallel.

India's Stake in the Rename

The renaming carries particular weight for Indian women. Prevalence estimates in India range from 3.7% to over 22% depending on diagnostic criteria and geography, according to studies published in JAMA Network Open and the Indian Journal of Medical Research. The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) was among the organisations that supported the global consensus study.

Dr Madhuri Patil, a Bengaluru-based reproductive endocrinologist and one of the Indian authors on the Lancet paper, told Medical Dialogues that the name change was overdue. "Basically it is a metabolic condition, and nowhere in the name was it mentioned that it is a metabolic disease, because that's the main feature," she said. "India is a major hub for metabolic diseases, with one of the highest incidences of diabetes mellitus in the world. So the name change is absolutely justified."

"I have learned a lot about PCOS after reading on my own and not from a gynaecologist. They are more interested in how it affects appearances and your sex life."

— Patient account, as reported by Forbes India

For Indian women in the diaspora, many of whom navigate healthcare systems where PCOS has long been under-recognised, the shift toward a metabolic framework could mean earlier referrals to endocrinologists and cardiologists rather than treatment that stops at the gynaecologist's office. Indian clinicians say patients frequently misunderstand the condition as being solely about "ovarian cysts," and the metabolic risks — particularly insulin resistance and diabetes — are routinely overlooked.

What Comes Next

Rachel Morman, chair of the UK patient charity Verity and a patient representative who helped announce the change in Prague, wrote in The BMJ that the rename was "the most comprehensive medical renaming process ever undertaken" — but cautioned that a better name alone changes nothing without follow-through in care.

Professor Teede echoed the point in Forbes India, noting that the media reach around the renaming has already touched roughly one billion people but adding that the name change is "necessary" yet not "sufficient." Updated research funding, broader medical education, and new treatment pathways will determine whether PMOS patients — particularly the millions in South Asia who remain undiagnosed — actually see improved outcomes.

For now, both PCOS and PMOS will appear in medical literature and patient-facing materials during the transition period. Health authorities in each country must individually decide when to adopt the change. But the direction is set: after 90 years under a misleading label, the condition has a name that finally tries to describe what it actually is.
